Superpower on Auto‑Destruct

Trump just “won” a 106‑day war with Iran the way a drunk “wins” by driving home without crashing: by pure luck and at everyone else’s expense. The White House calls it a decisive victory. 

Iran still has its regime, its nukes program, its proxies — and a new leader with the same last name. The U.S. calls the Strait of Hormuz “toll free” like it wasn’t exactly the same four months and 300 billion dollars ago. This is not strategy. This is pyromania with a press release.

The real damage isn’t just in Tehran. It’s in Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait, the UAE — the “string of pearls” of American bases that were supposed to be an ironclad security guarantee and instead turned into high‑value targets on a live‑fire range. Bases evacuated in a panic, command centers hit, families rushed out under fire. 

Allies look at their bombed airports and desalination plants and ask the only honest question: is hosting the American war machine protection — or an invitation to get hit first?

Meanwhile, Washington is doing what every dying empire does: lying to itself. Britain had Suez, the USSR had Afghanistan, America gets a 106‑day war with Iran that ends in a flimsy memorandum of understanding — the diplomatic equivalent of a first Tinder date — after “using the big stick” and proving it’s not that big anymore. 

The U.S. spends over 100 billion, hammers bases across the region, then scrambles to sign a cease-fire that gives Iran survival, leverage and symbolism: American “victory” literally burning on old bases in Iraq.

Allies see it. Spain, France, Italy, Turkey quietly slam the door on U.S. war access. Britain takes a drone hit on a base in Cyprus and discovers that “forward presence” means their small island is suddenly part of someone else’s war theater. 

Gulf monarchies watch their civilian infrastructure get hit and start hedging, not because China or Russia are better guardians, but because the American umbrella now looks more like Swiss cheese than steel.

Back home, Trump dresses retreat up as “optimization.” Pull troops from Europe, thin out in Korea, complain about 60,000 troops in Japan, quietly push hardware into Guam and Palau. It’s not grand strategy, it’s managed shrinkage with macho branding. 

The U.S. still has muscle, but no political will to pay the price of using it — and everyone can see it, except the people rehearsing their “mission accomplished” lines for cable news.

Call it what you want — “superpower suicide,” imperial atrophy, strategic burnout. The effect is the same: every new war sold as a show of strength ends up exposing how little control Washington actually has over outcomes, allies, or even its own impulses. 

The empire isn’t collapsing in one dramatic scene; it’s bleeding out through a thousand “limited operations” that don’t achieve their goals but do convince the rest of the world that betting everything on American protection is starting to look like the riskiest trade on the table.

'No limits' to my power, says man who can't even get Iran to show up to talks

In a moment of staggering self-regard, President Trump declared there are "no limits" to his power, brushing off the Iran war as a lesson he simply hasn't learned — because, in his mind, "we defeated them totally militarily." Never mind that the war dragged on, or that the "unconditional surrender" he promised Tehran turned out to be a vaguely worded memorandum that hands Iran $300 billion and sanctions relief in exchange for... more talks.

The deal he's now touting as a total victory is already falling apart — technical negotiations in Switzerland were postponed indefinitely as Israel keeps bombing Hezbollah, and even members of his own party are calling it the "worst foreign policy blunder in decades." But Trump is doubling down, insisting that a 14-point agreement with most details punted to "further talks" somehow amounts to Tehran waving the white flag.

It takes a special kind of delusion to call a deal that gives Iran nearly everything it wants while delivering nothing concrete an "unconditional surrender" — especially when the other side hasn't even shown up to the negotiating table yet. Trump lives in a world where saying something makes it true, where a piece of paper with no enforcement mechanism is a "historic breakthrough," and where his power has "no limits" — right up until reality inevitably proves otherwise.
